pages.text: As the U.S. Department of Defense expanded its Section 1260H list of “Chinese military companies operating in the U.S.” in June 2026, three dominant internet and technology giants — Baidu, Alibaba and Tencent (BAT) — have been flagged as an extension of the Chinese state and subject to the Pentagon procurement ban that excludes them from DoD’s supply chain. The listing also signals an increasing risk of further sanctions from the Department of Commerce or the Treasury. Alibaba protested the classification by suing the Pentagon . In the court filing , Alibaba denied any affiliation with the Chinese military or any role in China’s state-directed military-civil fusion strategy.

It argued that the listing and ban “has no basis in fact or law” and deprives the company of future business opportunities. It also argues that the abrupt announcement has violated the company’s constitutional right to explain its position. Section 1260H was introduced in 2021 to address the so-called Chinese state strategy of “ military-civil fusion ,” which facilitates the transfer of commercial tech companies’ technology or research to Chinese defense bases.

The DoD’s statement describes Alibaba as “indirectly affiliated with SASAC” ( State-owned Assets Supervision and Administration Commission of the State Council of the People’s Republic of China), and a “military-civil fusion contributor to the Chinese defense industrial base” because it is affiliated with China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT). Setting aside the debate over procedural justice, the public records — mostly international and Chinese domestic news reports — that the DoD submitted to the court as evidence of its decision largely reflect the authoritative nature of China’s big-tech governance, highlighting Alibaba’s strategic alignment with the Chinese government’s censorship, technology, and military development strategy.

Citing news reports about China’s censorship and Alibaba’s official document about its milestone in tech development in its submission to the court, DoD suggests the company plays an active role in building China’s censorship regime. Indeed, China has more than a dozen laws and regulations. The Cybersecurity Law (2017), for example, requires network operators to monitor, halt, and delete prohibited content; preserve logs; and report incidents to government authorities. Provisions on the Governance of Cyber Information Content Ecosystem (2020) classify content into three major categories: positive, illegal, and negative, and demand that operators promote, delete, and suppress them accordingly.

AI-related laws ban the use of algorithms to “influence public opinion” or encourage addiction/overconsumption, and ensure generative AI models adhere to the state’s “core socialist values.” Alibaba argued that compliance with Chinese regulations should not be interpreted as evidence of military ties, since all multinational companies operating in China, including American firms, must follow local laws.

However, the Pentagon’s public record attachment to the court suggests that Alibaba not only adheres to the censorship requirements in its consumer platforms, generative AIs, and mobile browser, but also develops censorship technology such as Alibaba “Green AI,” which automates real-time filtering across text, images, voice, video, and streaming data, and sells the content moderation tools to both domestic and overseas developers, e-commerce vendors, video streaming services, and gaming platforms, so that they can operate within China’s legal requirements.

Beyond assisting and exporting censorship technology, which is not for military purposes, the DoD’s court filing also includes news reports and commentary about the disappearance of its founder, Jack Ma, in late November 2020. Prior to Jack Ma’s disappearance, on October 24, 2020, he criticized China’s banking system as being outdated, and later, on November 3, Alibaba’s Ant Finance’s USD 37 billion dual listing in Shanghai and Hong Kong stock markets was suspended. His disappearance coincided with the Chinese authorities’ antitrust investigation against Alibaba, which was eventually fined USD 2.75 billion for forcing merchants to choose between platforms.

The DoD also suggested Alibaba’s “indirect affiliation” with SASAC and military ties through the company’s joint venture profile, in particular its joint venture with Norinco Group , a Chinese state-owned military company sanctioned by the U.S. Department of the Treasury, in establishing Qianxun Intelligence , which develops a spatial intelligence AI that uses the Beidou Navigation Satellite System and ground stations to deliver precise positioning for smart cars, drones, and mobile devices. Beidou is owned and operated by the China National Space Administration.

Although Alibaba relinquished its 50 percent share in Qianxun Intelligence in 2018, allegedly , its executive members still control a large stake, and Alibaba still relies on Qianxun AI for its commercial products. The DoD also noted that Alibaba partnered with China Mobile, a Chinese state-owned enterprise, to build data centers for cloud computing and AI. As Alibaba increasingly invests in these sectors, this partnership will likely only grow stronger, as such technologies heavily rely on data centers and geospatial technology — all of which are strategic sectors under the Chinese government’s national security framework.

Since 2026, Alibaba has entered a new power plant joint venture in coastal Ningbo city with state-owned China National Nuclear Power Co. to secure a stable electricity supply for its future data centers’ needs, and last month it acquired a stake in state-owned Shanghai Spacecom Satellite Technology to develop Qianfan Constellation (千帆星座), a low-Earth-orbit broadband constellation similar to SpaceX’s Starlink for its geolocation products. As a private company dual-listed in the U.S. and Hong Kong stock exchanges, Alibaba is not under SASAC supervision; however, amid the China-U.S. tech race, Alibaba’s investments inevitably fall into strategic areas that require working with state-owned corporates.

The DoD argues these ties include indirect affiliation with SASAC, catering to China’s civil-military fusion strategy. Moreover, some of Alibaba’s subsidiaries, including Shanghai-based Youku Film and Television (video streaming) and Guangzhou Lujiao Information Technology Co., Ltd have “golden shares” arrangements with state-owned enterprises backed by China Internet Investment Fund (CIIF) set up by the Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC) to strengthen the board-level management of Alibaba’s content platforms. The DoD cites the inclusion of high-level representatives from Chinese big tech, including Alibaba, Baidu, Huawei, and Tencent, in China’s AI Standardization Technical Committee under the MIIT as evidence of Alibaba’s direct ties to the Chinese government .

Citing analysis from the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) newsletter, Qiushi (求是), and various China observers from the West, the DoD’s argument is that Alibaba’s investment and development are strategically aligned with the Chinese government policy, which includes the installation of AI technology into its military hardware, the strategy of hosting data centers in western regions, building the space computing infrastructure, and more. Indeed, not only is big tech like Alibaba confined by the government; Chinese regulators’ sudden call-off of Facebook’s acquisition of Manus , a Chinese AI start-up, earlier this year reflects China’s fervor to secure and control its technology sector.

The current Chinese big tech governance model stems from decades of stability-control experience aimed at securing the single-party regime through censorship, surveillance, party-building, and ideological control. Whereas the development of AI has triggered anxiety surrounding automated crimes such as AI-hacking and unemployment in the West, China sees AI simply as a governable tool. For example, in response to waves of delivery workers’ strikes against AI pressure in recent years, in parallel with crackdowns and arrests, regulators also summoned representatives from major platforms, including Jingdong, Meituan, and Taobao, and instructed them to adjust their algorithms, abolish late delivery penalties, introduce rest time, and encourage labor-platform negotiations.

Taobao, Alibaba’s domestic shopping platform, has thus far established more than 300 party branches for 300,000 Taobao delivery workers , and, through these branches, provides on-the-job training, cheap accommodation and meals for workers in need, which is indeed a merit for the working class. In the ongoing court case, Alibaba argues against the DoD allegations, saying the company follows both Chinese and U.S. laws and is managed by an independent board of directors with no military affiliation. It also stresses that its core business, including cloud services, e-commerce, and logistics, serves commercial businesses and individual consumers rather than the military sector.
The case would test the U.S. government’s stance on the Chinese big-tech governance model. Tencent and Baidu have not yet filed any appeal to be delisted from DoD’s 1260H sanctions list.

pages.text: Thank you Orlaigh and the IIEA for hosting us today. I’d also like to thank the Irish Government, and the European Union, for inviting me to join today’s meeting of development ministers – the first time the UK has sat around that table since Brexit. Before coming here, I met Neale Richmond and we reflected on the strength of the relationship between the UK and Ireland. As nearest neighbours, we share common interests. But more importantly, we share common values – a belief in democracy, multilateralism, the rule of law, and standing up for those most in need.

Those values matter more than ever, because we are living through a period of profound uncertainty. Conflict is driving humanitarian crises across the world. In Sudan, Gaza, Ukraine, too many places, the level of suffering is immense. If you switch on the news today, you could be forgiven for thinking that the world is becoming a darker and darker place. But being here in Ireland is a reminder that darker days need not lie ahead. This country has a long history of refusing to accept that cruelty is inevitable. I travelled here today from Scotland.

More than thirteen hundred years ago, the Abbot of Iona made the same journey for a gathering he had convened on this island to establish the Cáin Adomnáin – the Law of the Innocents. Often described as Europe’s first human rights treaty, it sought to protect women, children and other non-combatants from violence. It reflected a shared belief that even in war there are rules, and that those not involved should be protected. Of course, warfare has changed enormously since then. Today’s conflicts are often more urban, more prolonged, and more complex. Yet some things have remained the same. Women and children still too often bear the brunt.

Human beings still find new ways to turn all our ingenuity into new ways to inflict harm on one another. And yet it is also the case that we have never lost the capacity to come together and agree norms and rules to protect life. Right from the days of the Law of the Innocents to the Geneva Conventions, the Mine Ban Treaty to the Arms Trade Treaty – each generation has tried to draw a line and say there are limits we will not cross. That is a tradition we must all hold on to.

Because development, humanitarian action and conflict prevention all begin with the belief that every human life should be cherished. And that brings me to my second point: we don’t just share a common humanity – we also share common challenges to that humanity. Whether it is climate change, access to decent work, whether food is affordable and accessible – the issues facing the young people in the Global South and the Global North differ in degree and not nature. That’s why I am determined that in how I do my job we will think of development not as something that happens ‘over there’ and not ‘over here’.

But as the process of ensuring that more and more of us are safe and have enough – enough to live well, and with dignity. That applies in Europe just as much as it does in Africa, Asia or anywhere else. It’s one reason I was struck by what Taoiseach Micheál Martin said during a UN General Assembly event we were both at last month – when he talked about Ireland’s long-standing commitment to tackling hunger and malnutrition, rooted in its values and experience. It reflected an understanding that solidarity begins by recognising ourselves in the experience of others.

That also helps explain why both Ireland and the UK continue to believe so strongly in international development – but also in doing development differently. For the UK, that means adopting a modern approach to development grounded in investment, stronger systems and local leadership – and rooted in shared solidarity and mutual interest. I’ll be thinking a lot about this as we prepare for the UK’s G20 Presidency next year. And that same spirit of shared solidarity brings me to the future of Europe’s role in the world – and the UK’s place within it.

The UK Government is committed to building a closer, more ambitious relationship with our European partners because as the Prime Minister said at the Labour Party Conference, Brexit has done more harm than good. So we are committed to reconnecting with our friends, allies and closest neighbours. My presence around the table of EU development ministers today is part of that. As I said, this is the first time the UK has been invited to this format since we left the EU, and we want to build on the discussions today and do so quickly.

We’ve also restarted formal development discussions with the European Commission, our teams in Brussels are working together more closely, and we’re looking forward to the second UK-EU Summit later this year. These are all important steps. But they are part of something bigger. A belief in solidarity across the continent we each call home and then onwards, ties of solidarity that tie the peoples of this continent to others around the world. There is so much that the UK and EU agree on. Not least our resolve to tackle poverty and injustice, respond to humanitarian crises, reform the international system, and build more resilient communities.
At a moment when some are stepping back from international cooperation, we are stepping forward. That is why I am pleased to be in Dublin today. And that is why today is just the start.

pages.text: A notorious illegal waste dump that blighted the beloved Kent beauty spot Hoad’s Wood has been completely cleared, the Environment Agency announced today, as the government’s crackdown on criminal waste gangs continues. The ancient woodland, a Site of Special Scientific Interest with rare plants and wildlife, had been targeted by organised criminals. They piled waste up to 15 feet high in places before officers shut the operation down. In total, 39,500 tonnes of commercial waste have been removed from the site, in an operation led by the Environment Agency and carried out by Acumen Waste Services Ltd. More than 50 specialist workers took part in the massive dig-out.

With the clearance finished, focus now shifts to healing the land. Access to the site will be restricted, giving nature the space and time it needs to recover. The Environment Agency is working with the Joint Unit for Waste Crime and Kent Police to track down the criminals behind the dumping, and three men have already been arrested as part of the investigation. This follows the Prime Minister’s announcement of a crackdown on waste crime, with the government and Environment Agency working together to ensure serious, organised criminal gangs have nowhere to hide.

This is another step in the government’s clean up of some of the country’s most egregious illegal waste sites, including Bolton House Road in Wigan and Midland Road in Bradford. These sites were prioritised on scale, risk to nearby communities, environmental damage, and links to persistent non-compliance and organised waste crime. To tackle waste crime at its source, the government is increasing the use of drones, giving Mayors and the police a bigger role, and introducing a dramatic rise in fines to deter those who dump illegally.

Alongside this, a new Waste Crime Crackdown Group, chaired by Environment Secretary Dame Angela Eagle, will bring regulators and law enforcement together to dismantle criminal operations and deliver results. The government is also giving the Environment Agency stronger powers to punish those who break the law. Rogue actors who dump waste illegally or fail to treat it correctly are set to face fines of up to £5,000, up from the current maximum of £300, while those responsible for serious offences can already face much tougher sanctions, including prosecution and imprisonment. Beyond fines and prosecution, the government will ensure that criminals pay for their actions in full.

The Environment Agency’s powers to confiscate cash, cars, houses and other assets bought with the proceeds of waste crime will grow, backed by new powers in the Crime and Policing Act 2026 to speed up confiscation orders. Through its 10-Point Plan on waste crime, the Environment Agency is also tackling illegal activity more widely, including suspending or revoking permits and naming and shaming illegal operators. The Environment Agency urges anyone with information that may assist the Hoad’s Wood investigation to call the 24-hour hotline on 0800 807060. Alternatively, the public can report it anonymously via Crimestoppers on 0800 555111 or their website.

pages.text: This article by Fabiola Chambi first appeared in CONNECTAS , in Spanish, on September 2, 2026. An edited version is being republished on Global Voices under a content partnership agreement. “We are sad, completely desperate. We have lost llamas, alpacas, sheep — we haven’t even been able to count them all yet […] That is how we make a living. We put our children through school and sell our products in the city.” The last heavy snowfall René Luna could remember had caught him by surprise nearly 25 years ago, but never anything like this .

A blanket of snow covered the landscape, and hundreds of animals were buried in his municipality in central Bolivia, which has now been declared a disaster zone. According to experts, this situation is a consequence of the phenomenon scientifically known as El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) , which in Latin America causes extreme temperatures or a lack of rainfall during the rainy season. This, in turn, leads to crop losses in rural communities, where farmers helplessly watch as months or even years of work are wiped out. The livelihoods of Latin American families depend on hard work in the fields, distribution systems, and access to food.

Unfortunately, this chain is becoming increasingly vulnerable as climate-related events disrupt it and worsen conditions in some subregions. In the 2026 edition of “State of Food Security and Nutrition in the World,” five international organizations reported that “25.8 percent of the world’s population (around 2.1 billion people) experienced moderate or severe food insecurity in 2025, meaning that at times [they] were forced to choose lower-quality or smaller quantities of food.” Paradoxically, the data showed a decline in hunger for the third consecutive year, meaning that improvements are possible, but they remain fragile and uneven.

Lena Savelli, Regional Director of the World Food Programme (WFP), explains that, to understand this phenomenon in relation to food security, three factors must be taken into account: first, conditions in the fields; second, prices and availability in the market; and third, families’ purchasing power and diets.

“What we will probably see over the coming months,” she predicts, “is that droughts or extreme rainfall […] will reduce the yields of key crops such as corn, beans, rice, and even cocoa and coffee, which will see their supply shrink and prices rise in markets and stores […] So, this means eating more expensive food with less variety, especially for those who already have low incomes. Families may find that the cost of their household’s basic food basket increases and that shopping becomes more difficult.”

However, Latin America and the Caribbean face a paradox, Savelli says: “It is an exporting region, but at the same time it has the highest cost in the world for a healthy diet: almost five dollars — exactly USD 4.91 — for each person per day. And people in this region do not have the income needed to feed their families; millions cannot afford to eat well. That is why we face a double burden of hunger, but we also have obesity, which impacts the economy.”

According to monitoring conducted by the WFP , several countries have already declared emergencies , and El Niño is expected to intensify during the second half of the year. For Jhenifer Mojica, an agricultural expert and former Colombian ambassador to the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), “smallholder family farming, including that of Indigenous peoples and local communities, is the backbone of food supply, but there is little awareness of how dependent we are on them.” She says that 80 percent of food security in Latin American countries depends on small-scale producers like these.

“An individual producer can hardly cope with this alone, and what we are going to see is an enormous amount of losses, as we are already seeing,” Mojica adds. “For example, the forest fires here in Tolima , a predominantly agricultural region where coffee, cocoa, fruits, and vegetables are grown. For a farming family, a harvest is not simply a harvest — it is the loss of their family’s assets.”

This phenomenon comprises three phases: El Niño, when the surface waters of the equatorial Pacific experience anomalous warming, which occurs on average every two to seven years and typically lasts nine to 12 months; La Niña, when those waters become colder than normal; and a third phase characterized by the transition between the two, with average temperatures — or temperatures within their usual range — lasting between one and six months. For Christian Domínguez, a researcher at Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México’s (UNAM) Institute of Atmospheric Sciences and Climate Change, this phenomenon has always existed because it is part of natural climate variability. Over time, however, it has undergone increasingly intense changes.

According to the World Meteorological Organization (WMO), the areas at greatest climate risk will be the Central American Dry Corridor (a belt stretching across Costa Rica, Nicaragua, Honduras, El Salvador, and Guatemala), the Caribbean, and northern South America, which will be particularly affected by droughts, water shortages, and heat waves. Meanwhile, Ecuador’s and Peru’s Pacific coasts could be affected by extreme rainfall and flooding, and doutheastern South America will experience above-average precipitation and severe storms. Many governments are moving fast to handle emergencies , but when it comes to effective prevention, there is a long road ahead. Savelli argues for tackling the structural causes: “It’s not just about producing more.

We have to confront persistent inequality, weak social mobility, and poor diets. Several countries in the region still struggle with high rates of child malnutrition, and we need to strengthen local food systems to make sure production actually reaches markets.” Some encouraging examples have emerged in Central America’s Dry Corridor, where alert systems now tell farmers when to plant, paired with practical prevention messaging . Climate insurance is another option, shielding people, businesses and governments from the economic losses that extreme weather causes. The risks extend to access to basic services, health (as mosquito populations spread), infrastructure, transportation and jobs.

As per the International Labour Organization (ILO) report “ El Niño 2026-2027 and the World of Work in Latin America and the Caribbean ,” informal, rural and outdoor workers are among the most exposed. As the report puts it, “El Niño 2026-2027 is, above all, a test of Latin America’s institutional resilience at a moment when external shocks keep piling up.” El Niño returned in June and its effects are already visible from space. New maps show concentrations of chlorophyll in the equatorial Pacific that are much lower than in other years, a signal of changes in the phytoplankton that sustains the marine food web.

As Domínguez adds, “We also have to consider that climate change is intensifying phenomena we already knew: droughts, heavy rains, heat waves, even cold waves. These existed long before, but by altering our environment, our atmosphere, we now face the consequences. So how do we live with this? We need to learn to adapt and respond through early-warning systems.”

pages.text: New UK humanitarian and energy funding will help bolster Ukraine’s preparedness ahead of its fifth winter under Russian bombardment. Arriving in Ukraine on his first visit as Foreign Secretary, Ed Miliband joined President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to the site of a recent strike in the Chernihiv Region which claimed the lives of at least 22 people, where he also announced fresh sanctions against Russia and £6 million funding to pursue justice for war crimes.

The strike site, a residential block in the city of Pryluky, which was badly damaged as part of an onslaught of drone and missile attacks sent by the Kremlin earlier this week, still has search and rescue teams present. Seeing firsthand the devastation caused by Putin’s war in Ukraine, the Foreign Secretary spoke with locals and emergency workers who had taken part in recovery efforts. During today’s visit the Foreign Secretary met both President Zelenskyy and Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha.

It came as Ukraine approaches the fifth winter of suffering under Russian bombardment and the Foreign Secretary commended the courage and bravery of the Ukrainian people in their fight for freedom. During his meeting with President Zelenskyy, the Foreign Secretary unveiled a sweeping package of sanctions against people and entities helping to support Russia’s war. The package, which includes around 40 targets across Russia’s financial, oil and technology sectors is designed to disrupt Russia’s supply chain and cut off financing streams.

The visits underlines the UK’s continued position: that Russia’s war is an assault on the core principles of the UN Charter and a demand of Putin and the Ministers who choose prop this up to move away from escalation and towards negotiations. Speaking from the ruins of the residential building, the Foreign Secretary condemned the scale of suffering. £54 million in combined energy and humanitarian funding is expected to support ordinary Ukrainians during the winter months - as Putin once again attempts to weaponize winter and plunge communities into darkness.

The UK is backing Ukraine through a triangle of support – bolstering Ukraine’s resilience; going after those who help to fund Russia’s war machine; and shoring up NATO security and meeting threats to our national security with robust action. Russian strikes on Ukraine have intensified this week, as just this morning a missile hit a bus in the eastern city of Kramatorsk, killing at least 30 people. Earlier this year as Ukraine suffered its worst winter in a decade, with millions plunged into darkness as temperatures reached –20c. The UK supported over a million vulnerable civilians by delivering much-needed generators and helping to repair damaged water and heating services.

The UK’s contribution today includes a £20 million to support Ukraine’s energy security, with funding for teams making emergency repairs to Ukraine’s energy grid following strikes, investment in back-up generators and solar power sources for blackouts and investment in new technologies to help Ukraine diversify power supplies. The package also includes £34 million to protect and maintain heating and water for Ukrainian families ahead of the winter and provide direct cash to support, working with the Ukrainian government and aid partners on the ground including UNICEF, UNHCR and the Ukrainian Red Cross.

Following his visit to Chernihiv, the Foreign Secretary returned to Kyiv where he visited a hospital where Ukrainian veterans were receiving medical care. The Foreign Secretary heard directly from soldiers who have served on the front-line, many returning with life-altering injuries. Here he announced £6.3 million of UK support for Ukraine’s domestic efforts to pursue justice and accountability for the perpetrators of heinous war crimes committed during Russia’s full-scale invasion. pages.text: The United Kingdom stands in full solidarity with Bulgaria, Romania and Türkiye following the attacks on civilian shipping in the Black Sea over the past 48 hours. Our thoughts are with the seafarers who have lost their lives, with those still missing, and with their families. The facts so far are these. On 5 October, the Turkish-owned cargo vessel Royad Mammadov, carrying corn from the Ukrainian port of Izmail to Italy, caught fire and sank in Romania’s Exclusive Economic Zone. Two crew members were killed. Romanian authorities rescued eleven others.

In the early hours of 6 October, two further merchant vessels, the Alfa Watan and the Able, were struck by air and sea drones in Bulgaria’s Exclusive Economic Zone. The Alfa Watan sank. Its crew remains missing. Eighteen sailors were rescued from the Able, two with serious injuries. This is the first such attack on shipping in Bulgaria’s Exclusive Economic Zone. The same day, a vessel carrying rapeseed oil was struck off Odesa, killing one crew member and injuring seven. We commend the Bulgarian and Romanian rescue services, and the crew of the ferry Dioscuria, for their swift response. We will follow closely the investigations now under way.

Mr Chair, these incidents did not occur in isolation. On 5 October, the Russian Ministry of Defence announced that its forces had struck two cargo vessels in the Black Sea. Attacks that fail to distinguish between military objectives and civilian vessels, or that are expected to cause excessive incidental harm to civilians and civilian vessels in relation to the anticipated military advantage, may violate international humanitarian law and the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea. The Russian Armed Forces must comply fully with its obligations under international law. The consequences reach well beyond the Black Sea.

Türkiye’s Chamber of Shipping has recorded 226 attacks on civilian and commercial vessels since the start of the war, the vast majority of them this year. Each attack raises the risk to crews of every nationality, drives up insurance costs and restricts the flow of food to those who depend on it. Among the crews affected this week were Turkish, Indian and Azerbaijani nationals. The UK is deeply concerned by the far-reaching consequences of successive crises across the global maritime domain. Stable and secure sea lanes are a global common good from which we all benefit.

Threats are drastically eroding international security, costing the lives of seafarers, and burdening the global economy – indiscriminately hitting the world’s most vulnerable. The international community must remain united in defending lawful commerce, protecting civilian shipping, and resisting attempts to use coercion against the global economy wherever it occurs. Mr Chair, this Forum exists to reduce the risk of misunderstanding, miscalculation and unintended escalation. When drones strike merchant vessels in the Exclusive Economic Zones of participating States, that risk grows. Russia’s illegal war against Ukraine has consequences far beyond the borders of Ukraine – it destabilises the whole of the OSCE area.

This week, it has reached the shipping lanes off the coasts of Bulgaria and Romania. In August, the Russian Foreign Ministry ruled out a ceasefire in the Black Sea. Ukraine has agreed to a full, immediate and unconditional ceasefire. The Kremlin has rejected it. The surest way to end attacks on civilian shipping is for Russia to agree to that ceasefire and to engage seriously in negotiations towards a just and lasting peace. The United Kingdom stands with Ukraine, and with our partners around the Black Sea, in upholding freedom of navigation and the safety of those who work at sea.

author: Ephraim Percy Kenyanito

pages.text: Kenya Judiciary building. Image by Wing via Wikimedia Commons ( CC BY-SA 4.0 ). This piece is part of Global Voices’ September 2026 Spotlight series, “ Protest in Democracy .” With this Spotlight, we seek to explore the many forms of protest, the tactics states use to delegitimize and suppress them, and the complex relationship between protest and democracy. You can support this coverage by donating here . On a Saturday in late July 2025, Angola shut down its internet for the first time in its recorded history. Not during an election, and not during a war. People had taken to the streets to protest the rising price of fuel.

At least 22 people were killed according to the authorities’ own figures; civil society monitors counted 30 dead and more than 1,500 arrested . I have kept a monthly record of technology, media and telecommunications law across Africa since January 2014 ; this August it reached its 152nd consecutive edition. Counting only entries where a government restricted, throttled or cut a network itself, and setting aside closures of individual broadcasters, I found more than 70 separate episodes across 32 countries, every year since 2014. Access Now’s KeepItOn coalition counted independently and arrived at the same number.

These events raise a question still debated in the abstract: What is digital protest, and do people have a right to exercise it? Typically, when thinking about online protest action, people picture hashtag campaigns, coordinated posting, online petitions, and a profile picture changed in solidarity. Using those examples, the right to the internet becomes a branch of free expression, and the argument becomes how much online speech a government must tolerate. Online protests are legitimate, and Africa has produced some of the most consequential campaigns: #ThisFlag and #ShutDownZimbabwe in 2016, #BringBackOurInternet during the Cameroon disconnection, #DataMustFall in South Africa, and in Nigeria’s #EndSARS 2020 and #EndBadGovernance in 2024.

In each of these cases, governments take one of two approaches and reach for a different instrument for each. The first approach is when a person posts, and the state prosecutes that person. I have found roughly 70 examples of exactly that every year since 2014, including Ethiopia’s Zone 9 bloggers in 2014, the co-founder of Jamii Forums under Tanzania’s Cybercrimes Act in 2016, Ignace Sossou in Benin in 2019, and two more journalists in Mali this June. Governments use cybercrime statutes, false-news provisions, or computer misuse acts to silence them, and the target is always a named individual.

The second approach is when many people gather, and the state prosecutes nobody. Instead, it cuts the network. Algeria has cut the national internet every year during the baccalaureate exams to stop candidates from circulating exam papers . Kenya blocked Telegram during its own national examinations in 2023 and 2024 . No crowd, no protest, no opinion the state wanted suppressed. So assemblies of dissent are not the only trigger, and an argument that says otherwise overstates its case. But notice what the exam shutdowns settle. Nobody claims Algeria switched off a national network to silence a view.

The state reached for the network because the network was what people would use to coordinate. A shutdown is not a speech instrument; it is an instrument for preventing coordinated action, and examinations and demonstrations are two instances of the same reach. Cut the network during a protest, and you have not silenced a conversation. You have dispersed an assembly before it forms. Viewing the right to the internet this way changes which provision of the African Charter applies, and what states owe their citizens. Shutdowns are almost always litigated as freedom of expression problems under Article 9 of the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights .

Article 11 protects the right to assemble freely with others. The two clauses are not the same. Article 9(2) gives everyone the right to express and disseminate opinions “within the law.” Article 11 permits “only necessary restrictions provided for by law.” Necessity is on the face of Article 11 and absent from Article 9. None of this is an African peculiarity. The International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights protects peaceful assembly in Article 21. In 2020, the UN Human Rights Committee, the body that interprets the Covenant, issued General Comment 37 , which sets out what that article means.

It reads Article 21 as covering assemblies held online, and the organizing of assemblies held in the street. On shutdowns, it is explicit: States must not “block or hinder Internet connectivity in relation to peaceful assemblies,” nor engage in “geo-targeted or technology-specific interference with connectivity.” That has been the settled reading for six years. The African Commission’s 2017 Guidelines on Freedom of Association and Assembly go further, treating assembly as something a state must positively enable rather than merely refrain from crushing. Its 2019 Declaration of Principles says at Principle 37(1) that states “shall facilitate” expression and access to information online.

Principle 38(1) permits interference with content where it is “justifiable and compatible with international human rights law and standards.” Principle 38(2), which prohibits “any disruption of access to the Internet … for segments of the public or an entire population,” carries no such qualifier. The asymmetry is deliberate, and it is doing far less work than it should. Cameroon’s Anglophone regions lost access for more than a year from January 2017 in a bid to clamp down on dissent. Fizi territory in South Kivu, Democratic Republic of the Congo, was offline for over a month from July 2026.

The Declaration is soft law, which is a real limitation; it is also the clearest statement of the continent’s standard on access rights. It is not just litigators who heavily rely on Article 9. It goes to the top. In 2024, the African Commission itself adopted a resolution on internet shutdowns during elections . The resolution treats a shutdown as harmful to expression and access to information under Article 9. It does not mention assembly at all. Ndiaga Gueye runs a Senegalese technology users’ association.

After the government cut mobile internet during the protests of June and July 2023 , he took Senegal to the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) Court of Justice . He pleaded for expression and access to information under Article 9, the right to work under Article 15, and assembly under Article 11 of the African Charter and Article 21 of the Covenant.

On May 14, 2025 , the Court ruled in his favor on grounds of expression, applying a four-part test of legality, legitimate aim, necessity, and proportionality and holding that Senegal failed on all four: no law authorized the cuts, no evidence of the threat was produced, fewer restrictive measures existed, and a blanket shutdown was neither necessary nor proportionate. It also ruled that the shutdowns violated his right to work. However, his claim that the shutdown violated his right to assembly went nowhere. Two applicants had brought it forward: the association and Gueye himself. The Court dismissed the association’s assembly claim because it was not argued or supported .

It accepted that Gueye was entitled to bring his claim, but then it decided the case on expression and the right to work, and never ruled on whether the government’s shutdown violated his right to assembly. The UN’s General Comment 37 had been in force for five years by then. That is the actual state of the argument. The assembly claim has been put to a regional court and gone nowhere, not because assembly is the wrong right, but because nobody argued it. Less than the advocacy suggests.

Zimbabwe’s High Court set aside the January 2019 shutdown directives within days , but on the ground that the minister of state had no power to issue them, the president having reserved the administration of the Interception of Communications Act to himself; the court expressly declined the constitutional question . The ECOWAS Court held Togo’s 2017 shutdown unlawful in June 2020 , but because Togo conceded that no law authorized it, the Court never reached whether a shutdown could ever be necessary or proportionate. In Kenya, Justice Bahati Mwamuye issued a conservatory order on May 14, 2025 , restraining a shutdown pending hearing, and by June rights groups were demanding compliance with it .

Zimbabwe and Togo are wins on legality rather than on the content of the right; neither tells a government what it may do once it has passed a law. Senegal is the exception: It is the first African ruling to hold that a shutdown fails a necessity and proportionality test. It reached that holding under Article 9, and failed to mention Article 11. Meanwhile, the shutdowns continued. Tanzania cut the internet during its October 2025 election and Uganda ordered a blackout before the January 2026 vote . Angola’s first shutdown in its history came 10 weeks after two courts ruled on the same day.

If litigators and human rights activists want to change this pattern, they must argue the assembly claim; not just merely list it. Gueye’s case shows what happens otherwise: The right was named in the pleadings and disposed of for want of evidence and argument, while the court went to work on the claims that had been built. The positive duty in the 2017 Guidelines is harder for a government to argue around than a proportionality test on content, but only if someone puts it in front of a judge properly. We must name the operators.

Shutdowns are executed by licensed companies on instructions that are frequently unwritten and sometimes unlawful under the licensee’s own domestic law. Civil society wrote to MTN, a leading telecommunications provider, about Sudan in 2019 . License conditions remain a lever barely pulled. Finally, we should treat non-compliance as an enforcement failure rather than an open legal question. When a Kenyan court restrains a shutdown, and the disruption continues, the deficiency is not in the law. The right to digital protest in Africa does not need inventing.
It needs locating, and governments have spent 12 years showing us where it sits: every time a crowd has gathered and the network has gone quiet.

pages.text: The UK would like to take this opportunity to respond to both Items 7 and 8 together. The UK is a strong supporter of the ECA, and we took note of the questions raised by Members at the July General Council. We welcome the Co-Conveners’ written response to those questions in document WT/GC/W/1006. I would add that this sort of questioning, and the responses that have been given, are very much what this chamber is for. The UK will continue to engage in that process.

If we do not respond to all questions that have been raised so far, we will do so going forward, and we should continue that discussion. This communication, together with the comprehensive statements provided by the Director-General at the July General Council and the Director-General’s communication JOB/GC/522 provides, we believe, a clear and factual response to the questions Members have raised in relation to the ECA and its implementation at the WTO. We would note that Members have always been able to conduct plurilateral activities at the WTO. These include areas such as the Working Group on MSMEs, Trade and Gender, Investment Facilitation for Development, and Plastics Pollution.

Doing so does not require consensus under the Marrakesh Agreement. We also believe that there is a strong institutional basis for the ECA and its implementation at the WTO. Irrespective of where the ECA was launched and negotiated, the intention always was, and remains to be incorporated into Annex 4, and it is very much rooted in the WTO and its institutions. Some have noted that the WTO Agreement is silent on whether the Director-General can play the role of depositary.

I would also note that the WTO Agreement is silent on whether the Director-General can form a FTA dispute panel, a function the Director-General plays in over 50 agreements involving more than 40 Members, none of which are WTO agreements. Thirdly, we would note that Secretariat servicing of ECA-related activities represents a continuation, not a change. In response to Members’ requests, the Secretariat provides logistical support for meetings, and facilitates technical assistance and capacity building. This is reflective of the sort of support the Secretariat provides to other groupings at the WTO. Again, I would note the MSME Working Group as an example.

At the Public Forum, we heard consistent expressions of support for the ECA from global representatives across all levels of development. The ECA is a prime example of the WTO delivering - or at least trying to do so - delivering for the real world and delivering for people around the world. It is an attempt to make progress on an important topic in a transparent and open fashion. Some Members have implied that we should simply pursue an agreement outside the WTO. I would note that all alternatives outside the WTO are less transparent, less open and less inclusive. This is the situation the UK is trying to avoid.

pages.text: The United Kingdom has listened carefully to Members today and over the past few weeks. We recognise many concerns have been raised. These include capacity constraints and also the need to ensure that all Members can see something of interest and value to them in this reform process. By return, the United Kingdom continues to want an inclusive process and is happy to look at ideas that support that. We will also engage constructively on issues beyond our immediate priorities, just as we hope others will do so. There is however an urgency to this work, which we cannot avoid.

The world around us continues to evolve and sadly doesn’t seem to be paying much attention to the WTO’s timelines. MC15, in that regard, is an important milestone. Whether we like it or not, it will be a point at which Ministers will judge whether we have made material progress on addressing the problems set out in the document that came out of Yaoundé, a document which all of us agreed in this room to work on, on a best-efforts basis, even though it wasn’t formally adopted.

We should also be clear that inaction has a cost, and the World Trade Report has shown that that cost could be considerable. We thank the facilitators very much for the hard work they’re putting in, the Members that have submitted reports and all those that have started the progress of engaging with them. title: Too young to run, old enough to protest: West Africa’s unfinished democratic bargain

pages.text: A section of young delegates at the West Africa Youth Democracy Conference held in Dakar, Senegal. 8-10 September, 2026. Photo by Legis360. Used with permission. In 2018, young Nigerians won a fight that had taken years to organise. The Not Too Young To Run campaign helped push through a constitutional amendment lowering the age limits for several elective offices. Eight years on, the legal victory has not made politics much easier for them. Party nomination and expression-of-interest forms can cost as much as 100 million naira (USD 75,000).

Earlier this year, one Nigerian state set the nomination fee for a local government chairmanship at NGN 30 million (USD 22,000), reportedly more than the office’s official earnings over a full four-year term. At the legal ceiling, election campaign spending is now at an all-time high in Nigeria. In February 2026, President Bola Tinubu signed the Electoral Act 2026 into law, doubling the presidential spending limit from NGN 5 billion to 10 billion (about USD 7.5 million) and raising the governorship limit from NGN 1 billion to 3 billion (USD 2.2 million). These are no small numbers for a young candidate.

That gap between being allowed to run and being able to run hung over a conference room in Dakar from September 8 to 10. Convened by the Economic Community of West African States ( ECOWAS ) Commission and Legis360 , the West Africa Youth Democracy Conference brought delegates from 12 countries together to discuss the barriers to young people’s political participation in the region. Nelson Asusiya , a young parliamentarian from Ghana, described a generation told to wait its turn while being used as poster children for political parties and civic movements, and rarely given actual power. Yet, the people being asked to wait are the majority.

Young people make up about 70 percent of the region’s population, according to the conference communiqué . Nelson Asusiya, a young delegate from Ghana, speaking at the West Africa Youth Democracy Conference held in Dakar, Senegal. 8-10 September, 2026. Photo by Legis360. Used with permission. Across West Africa , young people remain largely absent from decision-making bodies despite their demographic weight. Political parties remain important gatekeepers , controlling who gets nominated, how candidates are selected and, in many cases, whose networks and resources can carry them through an election. The Not Too Young To Run campaign in Nigeria showed what organised pressure can achieve.

But it also exposed that changing the rules is not the same as changing who can afford to use them. Cynthia Mbamalu , director of programmes at Yiaga Africa , which led the campaign, told the conference that while the amendment lowered the legal barrier, the political space remained more open on paper than in practice, with young aspirants still facing structural and financial barriers to contesting and winning. Ezenwa Nwagwu, a Nigerian civil society leader, called the result a contradiction: Young people are old enough to vote and old enough to protest, but are often told they need experience before they can hold political office.

He also rejected the idea that young Africans are impatient and drifting from democracy. Democracy, he argued, is measured not by its “dividends” of roads, hospitals and jobs, but by the freedom to question power. Across West Africa, protest has long been one of the ways citizens challenge political power. In 2012, Senegal’s Y’en a Marre movement mobilised young people against poor governance and President Abdoulaye Wade’s bid for a third term. In Burkina Faso, Le Balai Citoyen (“The Citizen’s Broom”) drew on young urban citizens to oppose Blaise Compaoré’s attempt to change presidential term limits .

These movements showed how street politics could turn constitutional questions into issues people could see and feel in everyday life. But protest has also met repression and contributed to distrust in formal institutions, as the #EndSARS protests in Nigeria showed. An estimated 577 protests took place across West Africa in 2020 alone, according to a 2025 study of social movements in Africa. The frequency of such mobilisation points to a region where citizens, particularly young people, are repeatedly demanding a greater say in how they are governed. But the region’s political institutions are themselves under strain.

On January 29, 2025, Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger formally withdrew from ECOWAS , the regional bloc that convened the Dakar conference. The three countries, all under military rule, had formed the Alliance of Sahel States (AES) and established a confederation in 2024, deepening a political rupture that has reshaped West Africa’s regional order. Director of political affairs, Dr Babatunde Afolabi, speaking at the close of the West Africa Youth Democracy Conference held in Dakar, Senegal. 8-10 September, 2026. Photo by Legis360. Used with permission.

For young West Africans, the withdrawal means millions of young people in Burkina Faso , Mali and Niger now live outside the regional bloc that convened the Dakar conference. Yet many of the questions discussed there: political participation, democratic governance and youth inclusion, remain relevant to them. Speaking with Global Voices in Dakar, Babatunde Afolabi , director of political affairs at the ECOWAS Commission, said negotiations with the Sahel states are progressing cautiously. He said: One of the benchmarks for measuring progress is the ability of the parties to engage. We’ve already started on that trajectory. It’s still early days.

He said a July summit in Freetown , Sierra Leone, called for the talks to expand to peace and security, because “we’re still the same people. Although the AES countries have left, we have a lot in common.” But the most concrete measure he offered was a year away. “One year from now,” Afolabi said, he wants the West Africa Youth Observer Network (WAYON), the conference’s main outcome, established, operating and partnered with ECOWAS. “That would be a good measure of progress,” he said. Nigeria’s campaigners proved in 2018 that young people can rewrite the rules.
The harder test, in Dakar and far beyond it, is whether anyone will rewrite the price. For now, getting through the door can cost as much as NGN 100 million (USD 75,000).

pages.text: We would like to thank the Secretary-General for his report. Upholding and promoting the rule of law, both at home and abroad, is a priority for the UK. As our Prime Minister made clear at the UN General Assembly, the United Kingdom will proudly stand up for our values and the rule of law. We remain a strong supporter of the United Nations, the UN Charter, and the Group of Friends on the Rule of Law. The rule of law is the cornerstone of any just, and prosperous society.

Not only does it play a vital role in sustaining peace by helping to address the root causes of conflict and insecurity, it is also fundamental to economic growth, enhanced security, and sustainable development. The rule of law creates the stability and legal certainty needed for investment and innovation. The UK Foreign Secretary, Ed Miliband, stated that we face a period of growing instability and increasing threats to international law and democracy. At such a time, the rule of law is more important than ever. We will continue to promote these values globally and do so in three ways. Secondly, by supporting the development of international law.

In times of crisis and global uncertainty, the rule of law is our anchor, it holds the international system steady and enables our multilateral institutions to function effectively. It underpins the legitimacy of multilateral action, giving those actions credibility and authority. We stand firm in our commitment to institutions that defend the international rule of law, and which tackle shared problems that threaten the resilience of the international system. Institutions such as the International Court of Justice are vital in ensuring that all States have equal access to justice and peaceful means to resolve conflict.

To ensure they remain relevant and effective, it is essential that we see the very best candidates taking up positions within them. That is why we are delighted to support Professor Dapo Akande’s candidacy for the ICJ. He is an outstanding candidate who would bring to the Court a distinguished record of expertise, as well as a global and independent perspective. It is important that everyone is able to contribute to the international rule of law, and the institutions that uphold it.

This is why the UK was pleased to contribute over £140,000 this year to the UN Programme of Assistance, as well as the ICJ judicial fellowship among others. Multilateralism and the rule of law reinforce one another as foundations of the international system. Addressing challenges to both requires an approach that promotes inclusive participation and fosters dialogue and diplomacy. This is why we welcome the UN80 reform initiative as a critical opportunity to refocus the organisation and bolster the UN’s impact. UN80 should result in a UN that is more efficient, effective, and coherent.

A UN that is better able to support governments to tackle the key challenges we face today. Secondly, the UK continues to play a leading role in shaping international legal discourse. For instance, the UK strongly supports the International Law Commission, as well as the dialogue with the Sixth Committee. We therefore contributed to the Trust on Foreign Assistance for Special Rapporteurs, to enable them to continue their work. We’re also pleased to chair the Steering Committee for the London Conference on International Law.

The 4th Conference was held in London last week, bringing together a global audience of international law experts from government, private practice, academia, and civil society to discuss current challenges. The UK takes a proactive approach to defending the international rules that underpin security and prosperity. For example, through our leadership on freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz to strengthen the international legal framework on which security and economic prosperity depend. Finally, we are committed to supporting accountability for the most serious violations of human rights and international humanitarian law.

The UK remains a strong supporter of the International Criminal Court and its independent role in holding perpetrators to account and achieving justice for victims. Accountability for the most serious international crimes has never been more important. The rule of law is not simply a principle; it is a priority. It is essential to sustaining peace, protecting human rights, and building prosperous and resilient societies.

pages.text: Drivers are set to save at the pump as near real-time petrol and diesel prices are included on Google Maps for the first time today (Thursday 8 October). Checking local fuel prices is now as simple as opening Google Maps and searching for a forecourt nearby, with near real time prices for petrol and diesel displayed on the app – supporting millions of drivers to access the cheapest fuel in their local area. At a time when the ongoing conflict in the Middle East has been pushing up fuel prices for drivers, comparing prices can save households who own a car around £40 a year.

This marks the latest step in the government’s work to tackle the affordability crisis, after the VAT cut to electricity bills and a £2 cap on bus fares, giving families some breathing space with the cost of living. The Fuel Finder scheme was created to help drivers get more competitive fuel prices following a recommendation by the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA). Since February, it has been compulsory for petrol stations across the UK to report the price of their fuel within 30 minutes of it changing or risk a fine – and the CMA can take action where there is evidence that petrol stations are not complying with the law.

The overwhelming majority of petrol stations are inputting data to Fuel Finder promptly, with around 99% of all fuel sold on UK roads now reflected. The data is already used by thousands of drivers across apps such as Waze, Petrol Prices, the AA, Confused.com and RAC Fuel Watch, and its integration with Google Maps will help millions more motorists find the best price at the pump. pages.text: When more countries join the European Union, we need to be ready. The new measures will prepare the European Union's governance , policies and budget for enlargement , while strengthening the protection of EU values and the rule of law . The EU can take in more countries within the existing Treaty and budgetary framework. Some improvements would, however, be needed in terms of administrative capacity and implementation .

pages.text: A reappointment has been made to the Board of the Water Services Regulation Authority (Ofwat). Iain Coucher has been reappointed as Chair for a second term, commencing on 1 October 2026. The appointment will run until the new integrated water regulator is established, and no later than 30 June 2029. More widely, this government is bringing tougher regulation, stronger enforcement, greater public control and accountability into the water sector, so water companies deliver for customers and the environment. The government intends to increase public control to deliver cleaner waters, fairer bills, stronger accountability, and better outcomes for customers and the environment.

Further details on the government’s approach to the water industry will be set out in the 10-year plan for Britain, to be published later this year. This will set out plans for stronger public control over essentials like water, making them work for people and places again, and will underpin the reform we will take forward through a strengthened Water Bill. During the transition to the new integrated regulator, Ofwat will remain fully operational and retain its existing legal powers while collaborating closely with Defra and partner agencies. This ensures there is no period without a dedicated regulator in place as the water sector moves to the new system.

Iain Coucher became Chair of Ofwat on 1 July 2022. He also chairs Ofwat’s Major Projects Committee and Nominations Committee. He is a senior adviser at HIG Capital, a Trustee of the British Trust for Ornithology and a Non-Executive Director of Charge UK. He has previously held senior executive roles including Chief Executive of the Atomic Weapons Establishment and Network Rail and has served as a non-executive director of Cadent Gas plc and a Board Member of the Rail Safety and Standards Board. The Water Services Regulation Authority, known as Ofwat, is a non-ministerial government department and the economic regulator of the water and sewerage sectors in England and Wales. Ofwat is responsible for ensuring that the companies it regulates provide consumers with good-quality, efficient services at a fair price.

pages.text: Barclays, HSBC, Lloyds, Morgan Stanley, NatWest, and RBC Capital Markets have been appointed as the Joint Lead Managers for the Digital Gilt Instrument (DIGIT) pilot issuance following a competitive procurement process. The appointment of Lead Managers is a key step towards the DIGIT pilot issuance, and these organisations bring expertise in both traditional sovereign bond issuance and digital markets. The Lead Managers will support the government by providing traditional Lead Manager services, including underwriting services, supporting investor engagement and distributing DIGIT on issuance day.

The DIGIT pilot, which is expected to take place by Q1 2027, will explore how distributed ledger technology (DLT) can be applied across the issuance and lifecycle of the bond. The pilot will put the new technology to the test—and show how the UK can turn its ambition for digital markets into practical action. Lucy Rigby KC MP, Economic Secretary to the Treasury, said: DIGIT is part of the government’s wider strategy to digitalise wholesale financial markets and keep the UK competitive as distributed ledger technology changes how finance works.

The Government is taking an active role in that shift, testing new infrastructure and helping create the conditions for firms to innovate and invest. Today’s (6 October) announcement follows the appointment of HSBC as the Distributed Ledger Technology (DLT) supplier in February, and the announcement in July that HSBC and LSEG (London Stock Exchange Group) have signed a memorandum of understanding to deliver a bilateral Digital Securities Depository link. The six Lead Managers were chosen following a procurement process that evaluated suppliers against transparent and objective criteria, and marks another major step towards delivering on our ambitions.

DIGIT will support the government’s commitment to maintain the UK as a world-leading and global financial centre. As other financial hubs explore DLT, the potential for significant growth in this area is clear. By launching now, the government is positioning the UK financial services sector to take advantage of this opportunity. The pilot’s design features include DIGIT being digitally native, short-dated, issued on a platform operating within the Digital Securities Sandbox (DSS), delivering on-chain settlement and independent of the government’s main debt management programme.

pages.text: Participants hold banners while security officers block them from marching in Phnom Penh during the May 1 Labor Day. Photo from Licadho. CC BY-NC 4.0 Cambodia’s Law on Peaceful Demonstration was supposed to ensure the right of citizens to organize and participate in public assemblies by designating freedom parks in every province. But since its passage in 2009, only one park has been identified, and authorities often impose prohibitions on the use of this space for protests. As early as 2009, several human rights groups flagged some of the restrictive provisions of the law.

The notification letter of the organizers of the planned demonstration will have to include a number of elements, including the number of participants involved in the demonstration. This requirement is absurd, since it is impossible to predict, ahead of a protest, how many people will join. If the estimates of the organizers appear to be inaccurate, under a strict interpretation of the law, the protest could be considered illegal. Amnesty International also pointed out that the law is silent on “spontaneous” protests. A related concern is the lack of recognition and protection in the [law] for spontaneous assemblies.

Spontaneous assemblies are those that occur without prior organization, usually in response to a specific event. Because they are unplanned, prior notification is not possible. In 2011, the Cambodian Center for Human Rights (CCHR) warned about the potential designation of freedom parks that are inaccessible to the public. Another concern with freedom parks is that they could be located where few citizens can see or hear those peacefully assembling or demonstrating, which defeats the object of demonstrations or protests, namely to voice concerns and express views, often in order to influence government leaders, local authorities and the general public.

The Phnom Penh freedom park became crucial for opposition groups to stage protests in 2013 and 2014. A new freedom park was named in 2017, but this was far from the city center and surrounded by warehouses and industrial buildings. “Moving Freedom Park to a location far from their [protesters’] target audience, resulting in a loss in the expressive value of assemblies, would therefore clearly impede the exercise of fundamental rights,” said the U.N.’s Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights country representative in Cambodia in an interview with VOA Khmer news outlet.

CCHR has documented numerous instances when the government explicitly prevented groups from holding protests in the Phnom Penh Freedom Park. For example, protesters from eviction-hit communities were blocked in January 2015. Barricades were placed in September 2020 ostensibly to maintain security and public order during the pandemic. UN Special rapporteurs issued a statement expressing concern over the security measures that undermined the use of the freedom park. This year, authorities denied permission for the use of the park to celebrate International Women’s Day and advised groups to mark the day by organizing activities in their respective offices.

The city also warned that organizers could face legal action if they proceeded to hold the event and “disrupted security, public order or social stability.” The same prohibitions were made during the May 1 Labor Day, and authorities only allowed ten people to walk and submit petitions to government agencies. CCHR cited the experience of groups in coordinating their plans with authorities. Authorities will call a meeting with CSO representatives, in which a small number of CSO staff will be greatly outnumbered by Government officials, many of whom are high-ranking.

Similarly, when the authorities call CSO representatives to hear their decision and explanation, the representatives are often not given sufficient time to speak or engage in discussion about the decision. It also summed up how the law has been weaponized to undermine protests. It has not only been used to confine peaceful gatherings and demonstrations to Freedom Park, but increasingly, the very use of Freedom Park has been restricted and denied. Restrictions on peaceful gatherings therefore risk limiting the democratic space in which Cambodians can exercise their agency and participate meaningfully in public and political life, reducing democracy to the act of voting alone.

Human rights groups are calling for the review of the law since more protests and assemblies are expected to be organized ahead of the 2027 Commune/Sangkat Council elections and the 2028 National Assembly elections.

pages.text: Most of England’s reservoirs are now classed as notably or exceptionally low after another dry month and the government is working with water companies to ensure supplies are protected. At this time of year, the Environment Agency would expect England’s overall reservoir storage to be almost three-quarters (74.3%) full. But because of this year’s drought most are less than half full, with concerns for Ardingly (West Sussex) and Wimbleball (Somerset) that are 23% and 21% full respectively. The updated statistics come after Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Environment Secretary Dame Angela Eagle both made clear this week that water is a priority area for the Government.

For the essentials of life, like water, the public interest should be the primary consideration - and this summer’s drought has underlined that need. On top of persistent action through the summer to coordinate across the water sector through weekly National Drought Group meetings, there will be wholesale reform of the industry through the strengthened Water Bill. More details will be set out in the coming months on the Government’s plans for water. The Government and the Environment Agency continue to scrutinise water company actions and ensure they are adhering to their statutory drought plans to conserve supplies and support communities.

As well as enhanced monitoring and more checks on abstractors, the EA is quickly processing drought permit applications to allow water companies to reduce the amount of water they must provide into local rivers. This means public water supplies are better protected, while also balancing the needs of the environment and local wildlife. South East Water is set to apply to the Government today (Friday) for a non-essential use ban (NEUB) that would leave more water available for households to prevent the need for additional measures. September is the sixth month this year that has recorded less than average rainfall, averaging 65% across the country.

However, there are significant regional differences with the drought-hit areas of England again seeing the least amount of rain. The east and south east saw 52% and 57% respectively. Central England saw 59% and the south west 69%. The cooler temperatures have seen demand for water reduce but we are still using more than expected for this time of year – putting reservoirs and public supplies under strain. Depending on rainfall and demand by consumers and businesses, reservoir storage is set to continue to decline throughout the rest of the year without major interventions – such as NEUBs.

Soils are still very dry and the Environment Agency recently warned that we need 120% of average rainfall over the coming seven months for the entire country to be out of drought by next spring. El Niño is set to put the UK at a slightly greater risk of a wet, stormy autumn but drought pressures will persist in some areas. Climate change means we are seeing an increase in both drought and flooding, and it is possible to have them simultaneously. Yesterday’s National Drought Group saw the EA announce two key changes to the way abstraction licences work to help farmers.

The moves follow the recent £65million funding boost announced by Mr Burnham over the summer. The first change allows farmers to start filling up their water storage reservoirs from yesterday (instead of November 1st), making sure they are prepared for continuous drought conditions. To protect the environment, this change will not apply to river catchments that are classed as principal salmon rivers to help fish stocks recover or those where S57 restrictions are in place. The second change makes it simpler for farmers to apply for longer-term abstraction licences. Environment Agency Chief Executive Philip Duffy, who chaired yesterday’s National Drought Group meeting, said:

A £65million package to help farmers impacted by drought, including funding up to £15million to build on-farm reservoirs, helping farmers to better store more water when it rains. £100million to strengthen the country’s capacity to respond to extreme weather and wildfires. Continued water company work on resilience, including nine new reservoirs by 2050 as well as desalination plants and multiple water transfers to help secure future supplies. Changes in the Planning and Infrastructure Act to enable non-water sector companies to build reservoirs that are automatically considered as nationally significant infrastructure projects, which will speed up the approvals for new reservoirs.

Continued work on mandatory water efficiency labelling; Defra will respond soon to a consultation on improving water efficiency in new homes. Continued work on nature-based solutions, such as restoring peatlands, creating more wetlands and planting more trees, to prevent flooding and hold more water in drought. Continued cross-government work on resilience to extreme weather, such as droughts, flooding, and wildfires. The National Drought Group - which includes the Met Office, government, regulators, water companies, farmers, Canal & River Trust, anglers, and conservation experts - is now meeting weekly to monitor the situation and coordinate action as part of the heightened incident response.

The Environment Agency is working on 10 Drought Permit applications, including recently granting South East Water a permit to help support Ardingly Reservoir. National Drought Group members are proud supporters of the Let’s Save Water campaign.

pages.text: Forty years of the global ban on commercial whaling was marked this week, as the government reiterated the UK’s long-standing opposition to commercial whaling at the 70th meeting of the International Whaling Commission (IWC). Whales, dolphins and porpoises have fascinated people for generations, and their presence in our waters continues to draw wonder and public interest. Protecting them for future generations remains a firm priority for the UK.

At this year’s IWC meeting – marking the body’s 80th anniversary and its 70th session – UK representatives secured further support for the protection of whales, dolphins and porpoises by co-sponsoring a resolution recognising the importance of cetacean strandings response and research, adopted by strong consensus. A cetacean stranding occurs when a whale, dolphin or porpoise washes up dead or alive on a beach or in shallow water. These strandings can reveal important information about the health of these animals, including why they died, and can point to wider risks such as pollution, entanglement in fishing gear, and vessel collisions.

To support this work, the UK has contributed £150,000 towards a new Global Cetacean Strandings Database, helping countries work together and share information more effectively. The new resolution will ensure that strandings data is used more effectively across the IWC’s work, leading to stronger coordination, better evidence, and faster responses when animals are found in distress. At IWC70, the UK also completed a two-year term chairing two of the IWC’s key committees: the Conservation Committee and the Scientific Committee.

Under UK leadership, the Conservation Committee has doubled the number of active Conservation Management Plans to ten expanded practical action on bycatch through pilot projects in five locations, and mitigation training in three locations. At IWC70, the Committee received a record number of national conservation reports, agreed a new Strategic Plan and vision aligned with global biodiversity goals, and agreed financial reforms to secure long-term funding for conservation work. The UK remains strongly opposed to commercial whaling and continues to call on the countries that still hunt whales to stop.

This international effort is matched by work at home to understand and reduce the pressures on whales, dolphins and porpoises in UK waters, including through the UK Cetacean Conservation Strategy and domestic strandings programmes. The IWC is the only global body with the authority to manage and protect cetaceans internationally, and the UK remains committed to working with other countries to help it do this effectively.
